n:
*Study note:* *Psalm 81*. The psalmist calls God’s people to assemble for a festival and then proclaims God’s message to them. The divine speech (vv. 6-16) recalls how God delivered the people from Egypt, reminds Israel of their rebellious past, expresses God’s desire for his people to obey him, and promises divine protection in exchange for obedience.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the Hebrew term הַגִּתִּית (haggittit) is uncertain; it probably refers to a musical style or instrument. See the superscription to {{Psalm 8|Ps 8}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the new moon.”

*Study note:* *New moon* festivals were a monthly ritual in Israel (see R. de Vaux, *Ancient Israel*, 469-70). In this context the New Moon festival of the seventh month, when the Feast of Tabernacles was celebrated (note the reference to a “festival” in the next line), may be in view.

*Study note:* The *festival* in view is probably the Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), which began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month when the moon was full. See Lev 23:34; {{Numbers 29:12|Num 29:12}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the full moon on the day of our festival.” The Hebrew word כֶּסֶה (keseh) is an alternate spelling of כֶּסֶא (keseʾ, “full moon”).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because a statute for Israel [is] it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in his going out against the land of Egypt.” This apparently refers to the general time period of Israel’s exodus from Egypt. The LXX reads, “from Egypt,” in which case “Joseph” (see the preceding line) would be the subject of the verb, “when he [Joseph = Israel] left Egypt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a lip I did not know, I heard.” Here the term “lip” probably stands for speech or a voice. Apparently the psalmist speaks here and refers to God’s voice, whose speech is recorded in the following verses.

*Translator's note:* The words “It said” are not included in the Hebrew text. They are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Study note:* *I removed the burden*. The Lord speaks metaphorically of how he delivered his people from Egyptian bondage. The reference to a basket/burden probably alludes to the hard labor of the Israelites in Egypt, where they had to carry loads of bricks (see {{Exodus 1:14|Exod 1:14}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I answered you in the hidden place of thunder.” This may allude to God’s self-revelation at Mount Sinai, where he appeared in a dark cloud accompanied by thunder (see {{Exodus 19:16|Exod 19:16}}).

*Study note:* The name *Meribah* means “strife.” Two separate but similar incidents at the place called Meribah are recorded in the Pentateuch ({{Exodus 17:1|Exod 17:1-7}}; {{Numbers 20:1|Num 20:1-13}}). In both cases the Israelites complained about lack of water and the Lord miraculously provided for them.

*Translator's note:* The words “I said” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Verses {{Psalm 81:8|8-10}} appear to recall what the Lord commanded the generation of Israelites that experienced the events described in v. {{Psalm 81:7|7}}. Note the statement in v. {{Psalm 81:11|11}}, “my people did not listen to me.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps “command.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew particle אִם (ʾim, “if”) and following prefixed verbal form here express a wish (GKC 321 §109.*b*). Note that the apodosis (the “then” clause of the conditional sentence) is suppressed.

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 81:9|9}} have a modal function, expressing what is obligatory.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “different”; “illicit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not listen to my voice.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew expression אָבָה לִי (ʾavah li) means “submit to me” (see {{Deuteronomy 13:8|Deut 13:8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I sent him away in the stubbornness of their heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they walked in their counsel.” The prefixed verbal form is either preterite (“walked”) or a customary imperfect (“were walking”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if only my people were listening to me.” The Hebrew particle לוּ (lu, “if not”) introduces a purely hypothetical or contrary to fact condition (see {{2 Samuel 18:12|2 Sam 18:12}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[and if only] Israel would walk in my ways.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turn my hand against.” The idiom “turn the hand against” has the nuance of “strike with the hand, attack” (see {{Isaiah 1:25|Isa 1:25}}; {{Ezekiel 38:12|Ezek 38:12}}; {{Amos 1:8|Amos 1:8}}; Zech 13:7).

*Translator's note:* “Those who hate the Lord” are also mentioned in 2 Chr 19:2 and {{Psalm 139:21|Ps 139:21}}.

*Translator's note:* See {{Deuteronomy 33:29|Deut 33:29}}; {{Psalm 66:3|Ps 66:3}} for other uses of the verb כָּחַשׁ (kakhash) in the sense “cower in fear.” In {{Psalm 18:44|Ps 18:44}} the verb seems to carry the nuance “to be weak; to be powerless” (see also {{Psalm 109:24|Ps 109:24}}). The prefixed verbal form is taken as a jussive, parallel to the jussive form in the next line.

*Translator's note:* The verb form at the beginning of the line is jussive, indicating that this is a prayer. The translation assumes that v. {{Psalm 81:15|15}} is a parenthetical “curse” offered by the psalmist. Having heard the reference to Israel’s enemies (v. {{Psalm 81:14|14}}), the psalmist inserts this prayer, reminding the Lord that they are God’s enemies as well.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and may their time be forever.” The Hebrew term עִתָּם (ʿittam, “their time”) must refer here to the “time” of the demise and humiliation of those who hate the Lord. Some propose an emendation to בַּעֲתָתָם (baʿatatam) or בִּעֻתָם (biʿutam; “their terror”; i.e., “may their terror last forever”), but the omission of bet (ב) in the present Hebrew text is difficult to explain, making the proposed emendation unlikely.

*Study note:* *I would feed*. After the parenthetical “curse” in v. {{Psalm 81:15|15}}, the Lord’s speech continues here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he fed him from the best of the wheat.” The Hebrew text has a third person form of the preterite with a vav (ו) consecutive attached. However, it is preferable, in light of the use of the first person in v. {{Psalm 81:14|14}} and in the next line, to emend the verb to a first person form and understand the vav as conjunctive, continuing the apodosis of the conditional sentence of vv. {{Psalm 81:13|13-14}}. The third masculine singular pronominal suffix refers to Israel, as in v. {{Psalm 81:6|6}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you.” The second person singular pronominal suffix refers to Israel, as in vv. {{Psalm 81:7|7-10}}.

*Study note:* The language in this verse, particularly the references to *wheat* and *honey*, is reminiscent of {{Deuteronomy 32:13|Deut 32:13-14}}.

*Study note:* *Psalm 82*. The psalmist pictures God standing in the “assembly of El” where he accuses the “gods” of failing to promote justice on earth. God pronounces sentence upon them, announcing that they will die like men. Having witnessed the scene, the psalmist then asks God to establish his just rule over the earth.

*Translator's note:* Or “presides over.”

*Translator's note:* The phrase עֲדַת אֵל (ʿadat ʾel, “assembly of El”) appears only here in the OT. (1) Some understand “El” to refer to God himself. In this case he is pictured presiding over his own heavenly assembly. (2) Others take אֵל as a superlative here (“God stands in the *great* assembly”), as in {{Psalm 36:6|Pss 36:6}} and {{Psalm 80:10|80:10}}. (3) The present translation assumes this is a reference to the Canaanite high god El, who presided over the Canaanite divine assembly. (See {{Isaiah 14:13|Isa 14:13}}, where El’s assembly is called “the stars of El.”) In the Ugaritic myths the phrase ʿdt ʾilm refers to the “assembly of the gods,” who congregate in King Kirtu’s house, where Baal asks El to bless Kirtu’s house (see G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 91). If the Canaanite divine assembly is referred to here in {{Psalm 82:1|Ps 82:1}}, then the psalm must be understood as a bold polemic against Canaanite religion. Israel’s God invades El’s assembly, denounces its gods as failing to uphold justice, and announces their coming demise. For an interpretation of the psalm along these lines, see W. VanGemeren, “Psalms,” *EBC* 5:533-36.

*Study note:* The present translation assumes that the Hebrew term אֱלֹהִים (ʾelohim, “gods”) here refers to the pagan gods who supposedly comprise El’s assembly according to Canaanite religion. Those who reject the polemical view of the psalm prefer to see the referent as human judges or rulers (אֱלֹהִים sometimes refers to officials appointed by God, see {{Exodus 21:6|Exod 21:6}}; {{Exodus 22:8|22:8-9}}; {{Psalm 45:6|Ps 45:6}}) or as angelic beings (אֱלֹהִים sometimes refers to angelic beings, see {{Genesis 3:5|Gen 3:5}}; {{Psalm 8:5|Ps 8:5}}).

*Study note:* The picture of God rendering *judgment* among the gods clearly depicts his sovereign authority as universal king (see v. {{Psalm 82:8|8}}, where the psalmist boldly affirms this truth).

*Translator's note:* The words “he says” are supplied in the translation to indicate that the following speech is God’s judicial decision (see v. {{Psalm 82:1|1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the face of the wicked lift up.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun יָתוֹם (yatom) refers to one who has lost his father (not necessarily his mother, see {{Psalm 109:9|Ps 109:9}}). Because they were so vulnerable and were frequently exploited, fatherless children are often mentioned as epitomizing the oppressed (see {{Psalm 10:14|Pss 10:14}}; {{Psalm 68:5|68:5}}; {{Psalm 94:6|94:6}}; {{Psalm 146:9|146:9}}; as well as {{Job 6:27|Job 6:27}}; {{Job 22:9|22:9}}; {{Job 24:3|24:3}}, {{Job 24:9|9}}; {{Job 29:12|29:12}}; {{Job 31:17|31:17}}, {{Job 31:21|21}}).

*Study note:* Having addressed the defendants, God now speaks to those who are observing the trial, referring to the gods in the third person.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “walk.” The Hitpael stem indicates iterative action, picturing these ignorant “judges” as stumbling around in the darkness.

*Study note:* These gods, though responsible for justice, neglect their duty. Their self-imposed ignorance (which the psalmist compares to stumbling around in the dark) results in widespread injustice, which threatens the social order of the world (the meaning of the phrase *all the foundations of the earth crumble*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said.”

*Study note:* Normally in the OT the title *Most High* belongs to the God of Israel, but in this context, where the mythological overtones are so strong, it probably refers to the Canaanite high god El (see v. {{Psalm 82:1|1}}, as well as {{Isaiah 14:13|Isa 14:13}}).

*Study note:* *You will die like mortals*. For the concept of a god losing immortality and dying, see {{Isaiah 14:12|Isa 14:12-15}}, which alludes to a pagan myth in which the petty god “Shining One, son of the Dawn,” is hurled into Sheol for his hubris.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “men.” The point in the context is mortality, however, not maleness.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like one of the rulers.” The comparison does not necessarily imply that they are not rulers. The expression “like one of” can sometimes mean “as one of” ({{Genesis 49:16|Gen 49:16}}; {{Obadiah 11|Obad 11}}) or “as any other of” ({{Judges 16:7|Judg 16:7}}, {{Judges 16:11|11}}).

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the Qal of נָחַל (nakhal) here means “to own; to possess,” and that the imperfect emphasizes a general truth. Another option is to translate the verb as future, “for you will take possession of all the nations” (cf. NIV “all the nations are your inheritance”).

*Study note:* *Psalm 83*. The psalmist asks God to deliver Israel from the attacks of foreign nations. Recalling how God defeated Israel’s enemies in the days of Deborah and Gideon, he prays that the hostile nations would be humiliated.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not be deaf.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lift up [their] head[s].” The phrase “lift up [the] head” here means “to threaten; to be hostile,” as in {{Judges 8:28|Judg 8:28}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they make crafty a plot.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and consult together against.”

*Translator's note:* The passive participle of the Hebrew verb צָפַן (tsafan, “to hide”) is used here in the sense of “treasured; cherished.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we will cause them to disappear from [being] a nation.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they consult [with] a heart together.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “cut a covenant.”

*Translator's note:* The words “it includes” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* The *Hagrites* are also mentioned in 1 Chr 5:10, 19-20.

*Study note:* Some identify *Gebal* with the Phoenician coastal city of Byblos (see {{Ezekiel 27:9|Ezek 27:9}}, where the name is spelled differently), though others locate this site south of the Dead Sea (see BDB 148 s.v. גְּבַל; *HALOT* 174 s.v. גְּבַל).

*Study note:* The *descendants of Lot* were the Moabites and Ammonites.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they are an arm for the sons of Lot.” The “arm” is here a symbol of military might.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do to them like Midian.”

*Study note:* The psalmist alludes here to Gideon’s victory over the Midianites (see {{Judges 7|Judg 7-8}}) and to Barak’s victory over Jabin’s army, which was led by his general Sisera ({{Judges 4|Judg 4-5}}).

*Study note:* *Endor* is not mentioned in the accounts of Gideon’s or Barak’s victories, but both battles took place in the general vicinity of the town. (See Y. Aharoni and M. Avi-Yonah, *The Macmillan Bible Atlas*, 46, 54.) Because Sisera and Jabin are mentioned in v. {{Psalm 83:9|9b}}, many understand them to be the subject of the verbs in v. {{Psalm 83:10|10}}, though they relate v. {{Psalm 83:10|10}} to Gideon’s victory, which is referred to in v. {{Psalm 83:9|9a}}, {{Psalm 83:11|11}}. (See, for example, Y. Aharoni, *The Land of the Bible*, 263.)

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they were manure.” In addition to this passage, corpses are compared to manure in {{2 Kings 9:37|2 Kgs 9:37}}; Jer 8:2; 9:21; 16:4; 25:33.

*Study note:* *Oreb and Zeeb* were the generals of the Midianite army that was defeated by Gideon. The Ephraimites captured and executed both of them and sent their heads to Gideon ({{Judges 7:24|Judg 7:24-25}}).

*Study note:* *Zebah and Zalmunna* were the Midianite kings. Gideon captured them and executed them ({{Judges 8:1|Judg 8:1-21}}).

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that “Zebah and Zalmunna” are the antecedents of the relative pronoun (“who [said]”). Another option is to take “their nobles…all their rulers” as the antecedent and to translate, “those who say.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let’s take possession for ourselves.”

*Translator's note:* Or “tumbleweed.” The Hebrew noun גַּלְגַּל (galgal) refers to a “wheel” or, metaphorically, to a whirling wind (see {{Psalm 77:18|Ps 77:18}}). If taken in the latter sense here, one could understand the term as a metonymical reference to dust blown by a whirlwind (cf. NRSV “like whirling dust”). However, *HALOT* 190 s.v. II גַּלְגַּל understands the noun as a homonym referring to a “dead thistle” here and in {{Isaiah 17:13|Isa 17:13}}. The parallel line, which refers to קַשׁ (qash, “chaff”), favors this interpretation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before.”
*Study note:* The imagery of *fire* and *flames* suggests unrelenting, destructive judgment.
*Translator's note:* The two imperfect verbal forms in v. {{Psalm 83:15|15}} express the psalmist’s wish or prayer.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fill.”

*Translator's note:* After the preceding imperative, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav (ו) indicates purpose or result (“then they will seek”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your name,” which stands here for God’s person.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and may they be terrified to perpetuity.” The Hebrew expression עֲדֵי־עַד (ʿade ʿad, “to perpetuity”) can mean “forevermore” (see {{Psalm 92:7|Pss 92:7}}; {{Psalm 132:12|132:12}}, {{Psalm 132:14|14}}), but here it may be used hyperbolically, for the psalmist asks that the experience of judgment might lead the nations to recognize (v. {{Psalm 83:18|18}}) and even to seek (v. {{Psalm 83:16|16}}) God.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “may they be ashamed and perish.” The four prefixed verbal forms in this verse are understood as jussives. The psalmist concludes his prayer with an imprecation, calling severe judgment down on his enemies. The strong language of the imprecation seems to run contrary to the positive outcome of divine judgment envisioned in v. {{Psalm 83:16|16b}}. Perhaps the language of v. {{Psalm 83:17|17}} is overstated for effect. Another option is that v. {{Psalm 83:16|16b}} expresses an ideal, while the strong imprecation of vv. {{Psalm 83:17|17-18}} anticipates reality. It would be nice if the defeated nations actually pursued a relationship with God, but if judgment does not bring them to that point, the psalmist asks that they be annihilated so that they might at least be forced to acknowledge God’s power.

*Translator's note:* After the preceding jussives (v. {{Psalm 83:17|17}}), the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav (ו) indicates purpose (“so that they may know”) or result.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that you, your name [is] the Lord, you alone.”

*Study note:* The divine title “Most High” (עֶלְיוֹן ʿelyon) pictures God as the exalted ruler of the universe who vindicates the innocent and judges the wicked. See especially {{Psalm 7:17|Pss 7:17}}; {{Psalm 9:2|9:2}}; {{Psalm 18:13|18:13}}; {{Psalm 21:7|21:7}}; {{Psalm 47:2|47:2}}.

*Study note:* *Psalm 84*. The psalmist expresses his desire to be in God’s presence in the Jerusalem temple, for the Lord is the protector of his people.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the Hebrew term הַגִּתִּית (haggittit) is uncertain; it probably refers to a musical style or instrument.

*Translator's note:* Or “your dwelling place[s].” The plural form of the noun may indicate degree or quality; this is the Lord’s special dwelling place (see {{Psalm 43:3|Pss 43:3}}; {{Psalm 46:4|46:4}}; {{Psalm 132:5|132:5}}, {{Psalm 132:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* Traditionally, “Lord of hosts.” The title draws attention to God’s sovereign position (see {{Psalm 69:6|Ps 69:6}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my soul longs, it even pines for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the courts of the Lord” (see {{Psalm 65:4|Ps 65:4}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my flesh,” which stands for his whole person and being.

*Translator's note:* The word translated “swallow” occurs only here and in {{Proverbs 26:2|Prov 26:2}}.

*Study note:* The psalmist here romanticizes the temple as a place of refuge and safety. As he thinks of the *birds* nesting near its roof, he envisions them finding protection in God’s presence.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “even a bird finds a home, and a swallow a nest for herself, [in] which she places her young.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun is an abstract plural. The word often refers metonymically to the happiness that God-given security and prosperity produce (see v. {{Psalm 84:12|12}} and {{Psalm 1:1|Pss 1:1}}; {{Psalm 2:12|2:12}}; {{Psalm 34:9|34:9}}; {{Psalm 41:1|41:1}}; {{Psalm 65:4|65:4}}; {{Psalm 89:15|89:15}}; {{Psalm 106:3|106:3}}; {{Psalm 112:1|112:1}}; {{Psalm 127:5|127:5}}; {{Psalm 128:1|128:1}}; {{Psalm 144:15|144:15}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man.” Hebrew literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle stated here was certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the plural “those.” The individual referred to in v. {{Psalm 84:5|5a}} is representative of followers of God, as the use of plural forms in vv. 5b-7 indicates.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “roads [are] in their heart[s].” The roads are here those that lead to Zion (see v. {{Psalm 84:7|7}}).

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the Hebrew phrase עֵמֶק הַבָּכָא (ʿemeq habbakhaʾ) is the name of an otherwise unknown arid valley through which pilgrims to Jerusalem passed. The term בָּכָא (bakhaʾ) may be the name of a particular type of plant or shrub that grew in this valley. O. Borowski (*Agriculture in Iron Age Israel*, 130) suggests it is the black mulberry. Some take the phrase as purely metaphorical and relate בָּכָא to the root בָּכָה (bakhah, “to weep”). In this case one might translate, “the valley of weeping” or “the valley of affliction.”

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “a spring they make it,” but this makes little sense. Many medieval Hebrew mss, as well as the LXX, understand God to be the subject and the valley to be the object, “he [God] makes it [the valley] [into] a spring.”

*Translator's note:* This rare word may refer to the early (or autumn) rains (see Joel 2:23).

*Study note:* *Pools of water*. Because water is so necessary for life, it makes an apt symbol for divine favor and blessing. As the pilgrims traveled to Jerusalem, God provided for their physical needs and gave them a token of his favor and of the blessings awaiting them at the temple.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads בְּרָכוֹת (berakhot, “blessings”) but the preceding reference to a “spring” favors an emendation to בְּרֵכוֹת (berekhot, “pools”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they go from strength to strength.” The phrase “from strength to strength” occurs only here in the OT. With a verb of motion, the expression “from [common noun] to [same common noun]” normally suggests movement from one point to another or through successive points (see {{Numbers 36:7|Num 36:7}}; 1 Chr 16:20; 17:5; {{Psalm 105:13|Ps 105:13}}; Jer 25:32). {{Psalm 84:7|Ps 84:7}} may be emphasizing that the pilgrims move successively from one “place of strength” to another as they travel toward Jerusalem. All along the way they find adequate provisions and renewed energy for the trip.

*Translator's note:* The psalmist returns to the singular (see v. {{Psalm 84:5|5a}}), which he uses in either a representative or distributive (“each one”) sense.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Lord, God, hosts.” One expects the construct form אֱלֹהֵי before צְבָאוֹת (tsevaʾot, “hosts”; see {{Psalm 89:9|Ps 89:9}}) but יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים (yehvah ʾelohim) precedes צְבָאוֹת in {{Psalm 59:5|Pss 59:5}} and {{Psalm 80:4|80:4}}, {{Psalm 80:19|19}} as well.

*Translator's note:* The phrase “our shield” refers metaphorically to the Davidic king, who, as God’s vice-regent, was the human protector of the people. Note the parallelism with “your anointed one” here and with “our king” in {{Psalm 89:18|Ps 89:18}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look [on] the face of your anointed one.” The Hebrew phrase מְשִׁיחֶךָ (meshikhekha, “your anointed one”) refers here to the Davidic king (see {{Psalm 2:2|Pss 2:2}}; {{Psalm 18:50|18:50}}; {{Psalm 20:6|20:6}}; {{Psalm 28:8|28:8}}; {{Psalm 89:38|89:38}}, {{Psalm 89:51|51}}; {{Psalm 132:10|132:10}}, {{Psalm 132:17|17}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “better is a day in your courts than a thousand [spent elsewhere].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I choose being at the entrance of the house of my God over living in the tents of the wicked.” The verb סָפַף (safaf) appears only here in the OT; it is derived from the noun סַף (saf, “threshold”). Traditionally some have interpreted this as a reference to being a doorkeeper at the temple, though some understand it to mean “lie as a beggar at the entrance to the temple” (see *HALOT* 765 s.v. ספף).

*Translator's note:* The verb דּוּר (dur, “to live”) occurs only here in the OT.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[is] a sun and a shield.” The epithet “sun,” though rarely used of Israel’s God in the OT, was a well-attested royal title in the ancient Near East. For several examples from Ugaritic texts, the Amarna letters, and Assyrian royal inscriptions, see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Psalm 18|Psalm 18}}/{{2 Samuel 22|2 Samuel 22}}” (Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983), 131, n. 2.

*Translator's note:* Or “grace.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he does not withhold good to those walking in integrity.”

*Translator's note:* Traditionally “Lord of hosts.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Oh] the happiness [of] the man [who] trusts in you.” Hebrew literature often assumes and reflects the male-oriented perspective of ancient Israelite society. The principle stated here is certainly applicable to all people, regardless of their gender or age. To facilitate modern application, we translate the gender and age specific “man” with the plural “those.” The individual referred to here is representative of all followers of God, as the use of the plural form in v. {{Psalm 84:12|12b}} indicates.

*Study note:* *Psalm 85*. God’s people recall how he forgave their sins in the past, pray that he might now restore them to his favor, and anticipate renewed blessings.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you turned with a turning [toward] Jacob.” The Hebrew term שְׁבוּת (shevut) is apparently a cognate accusative of שׁוּב (shuv). See {{Psalm 14:7|Pss 14:7}}; {{Psalm 53:6|53:6}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the rage of your anger.” The phrase “rage of your anger” employs an appositional genitive. Synonyms are joined in a construct relationship to emphasize the single idea. For a detailed discussion of the grammatical point with numerous examples, see Y. Avishur, “Pairs of Synonymous Words in the Construct State (and in Appositional Hendiadys) in Biblical Hebrew,” *Semitics* 2 (1971): 17-81. See {{Psalm 69:24|Pss 69:24}}; {{Psalm 78:49|78:49}}.

In this case one may read “God.” Some, following a Qumran text and the LXX, also propose the phrase occurred in the original text of {{Deuteronomy 32:8|Deut 32:8}}. The phrase בְנֵי אֵלִים (vene ʾelim, “sons of gods” or “sons of God”) occurs only here and in {{Psalm 29:1|Ps 29:1}}. Since the “sons of gods/God” are here associated with “the assembly of the holy ones” and “council of the holy ones,” the heavenly assembly (comprised of so-called “angels” and other supernatural beings) appears to be in view. See {{Job 5:1|Job 5:1}}; {{Job 15:15|15:15}} and Zech 14:5, where these supernatural beings are referred to as “holy ones.” In Canaanite mythological texts the divine council of the high god El is called “the sons of El.” The OT apparently uses the Canaanite phrase, applying it to the supernatural beings that surround the Lord’s heavenly throne.

However, the name is also used of the sea (or the mythological sea creature) which symbolizes the disruptive forces of the world that seek to replace order with chaos (see {{Job 9:13|Job 9:13}}; {{Job 26:12|26:12}}). {{Isaiah 51:9|Isa 51:9}} appears to combine the mythological and historical referents. The association of Rahab with the sea in {{Psalm 89|Ps 89}} (see v. {{Psalm 89:9|9}}) suggests that the name carries symbolic force in this context. In this case the passage may allude to creation (see vv. {{Psalm 89:11|11-12}}), when God overcame the great deep and brought order out of chaos.

*Study note:* The basic sense of the word “holy” is “set apart from that which is commonplace, special, unique.” The Lord’s holiness is first and foremost his transcendent sovereignty as the ruler of the world. He is “set apart” from the world over which he rules. At the same time his holiness encompasses his moral authority, which derives from his royal position. As king he has the right to dictate to his subjects how they are to live; indeed his very own character sets the standard for proper behavior. This expression is a common title for the Lord in the book of Isaiah.

Such gifts usually took the form of land and/or an enduring dynasty. See M. Weinfeld, “The Covenant of Grant in the Old Testament and in the Ancient Near East,” *JAOS* 90 (1970): 184-203, for general discussion and some striking extra-biblical parallels.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a witness in the sky, secure.” Scholars have offered a variety of opinions as to the identity of the “witness” referred to here, none of which is very convincing. It is preferable to join וְעֵד (veʿed) to עוֹלָם (ʿolam) in the preceding line and translate the commonly attested phrase עוֹלָם וְעֵד (“forever”). In this case one may translate the second line, “[it] will be secure like the skies.” Another option (the one reflected in the present translation) is to take עד as a rare noun meaning “throne” or “dais.” This noun is attested in Ugaritic; see, for example, CTA 16 vi 22-23, where ksi (= כִּסֵּא, kisseʾ, “throne”) and ʿd (= עד, “dais”) appear as synonyms in the poetic parallelism (see G. R. Driver, *Canaanite Myths and Legends*, 91). Emending בַּשַּׁחַק (bashakhaq, “in the heavens”) to כַּשַׁחַק (kashakhaq, “like the heavens”)—bet*/*kaf (כ/ב) confusion is widely attested—one can then read “[his] throne like the heavens [is] firm/stable.” Verse {{Psalm 89:29|29}} refers to the enduring nature of the heavens, while {{Job 37:18|Job 37:18}} speaks of God spreading out the heavens (שְׁחָקִים, shekhaqim) and compares their strength to a bronze mirror. {{Psalm 89:29|Ps 89:29}} uses the term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim, “skies”) which frequently appears in parallelism to שְׁחָקִים.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew construction (conjunction + pronoun, followed by the verb) draws attention to the contrast between what follows and what precedes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your anointed one.” The Hebrew phrase מְשִׁיחֶךָ (meshikhekha, “your anointed one”) refers here to the Davidic king (see {{Psalm 2:2|Pss 2:2}}; {{Psalm 18:50|18:50}}; {{Psalm 20:6|20:6}}; {{Psalm 28:8|28:8}}; {{Psalm 84:9|84:9}}; {{Psalm 132:10|132:10}}, {{Psalm 132:17|17}}).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb appears only here and in Lam 2:7.

*Translator's note:* The perfect verbal form predominates in vv. {{Psalm 89:38|38-45}}. The use of the imperfect in this one instance may be for rhetorical effect. The psalmist briefly lapses into dramatic mode, describing the king’s military defeat as if it were happening before his very eyes.

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “you turn back, rocky summit, his sword.” The Hebrew term צוּר (tsur, “rocky summit”) makes no sense here, unless it is a divine title understood as vocative, “you turn back, O Rocky Summit, his sword.” Some emend the form to צֹר (tsor, “flint”) on the basis of {{Joshua 5:2|Josh 5:2}}, which uses the phrase חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים (kharvot tsurim, “flint knives”). The noun צֹר (tsor, “flint”) can then be taken as “flint-like edge,” indicating the sharpness of the sword. Others emend the form to אָחוֹר (ʾakhor, “backward”) or to מִצַּר (mitsar, “from the adversary”). The present translation reflects the latter, assuming an original reading תָּשִׁיב מִצָּר חַרְבּוֹ (tashiv mitsar kharbo), which was changed to תָּשִׁיב צָר חַרְבּוֹ (tashiv tsar kharbo) by virtual haplography (confusion of *bet/mem* is well-attested) with צָר (tsar, “adversary”) then being misinterpreted as צוּר in the later tradition.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who [is] the man [who] can live and not see death, [who] can deliver his life from the hand of Sheol?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “No one!”

*Study note:* The final verse of {{Psalm 89|Ps 89}}, v. {{Psalm 89:52|52}}, is a conclusion to this third “book” (or major editorial division) of the Psalter. Similar statements appear at or near the end of each of the first, second and fourth “books” of the Psalter (see {{Psalm 41:13|Pss 41:13}}; {{Psalm 72:18|72:18-19}}; {{Psalm 106:48|106:48}}, respectively).

*Study note:* *Psalm 90*. In this communal lament the worship leader affirms that the eternal God and creator of the world has always been Israel’s protector. But God also causes men, who are as transient as grass, to die, and in his fierce anger he decimates his covenant community, whose brief lives are filled with suffering and end in weakness. The community asks for wisdom, the restoration of God’s favor, a fresh revelation of his power, and his blessing upon their labors.

*Translator's note:* Or “place of safety.” See {{Psalm 71:3|Ps 71:3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and you gave birth to the earth and world.” The Polel verbal form in the Hebrew text pictures God giving birth to the world. The LXX and some other ancient textual witnesses assume a Polal (passive) verbal form here. In this case the earth becomes the subject of the verb and the verb is understood as third feminine singular rather than second masculine singular.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and from everlasting to everlasting you [are] God.” Instead of אֵל (ʾel, “God”) the LXX reads אַל (ʾal, “not”) and joins the negative particle to the following verse, making the verb תָּשֵׁב (tashev) a jussive. In this case v. {{Psalm 90:3|3a}} reads as a prayer, “do not turn man back to a low place.” However, taking תָּשֵׁב as a jussive is problematic in light of the following wayyiqtol form וַתֹּאמֶר (vatoʾmer, “and you said/say”), unless one reads the form as a simple vav plus imperfect as indicated by Aquila and Jerome.

*Translator's note:* In this context the shortened prefix form does not function as a preterite, but indicates what is typical of the world.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term דַּכָּא (dakaʾ) carries the basic sense of “crushed.” Elsewhere it refers to those who are “crushed” in spirit or contrite of heart (see {{Psalm 34:18|Ps 34:18}}; {{Isaiah 57:15|Isa 57:15}}). If one understands this nuance here, then v. {{Psalm 90:3|3}} is observing that God leads mankind to repentance (the term שׁוּב, shuv, “return,” which appears twice in this verse, is sometimes used of repentance.) However, the following context laments mankind’s mortality and the brevity of life, so it is doubtful if v. {{Psalm 90:3|3}} should be understood so positively. It is more likely that דַּכָּא here refers to “crushed matter,” that is, the dust that fills the grave (see *HALOT* 221 s.v. s.v. I דַּכָּא; BDB 194 s.v. דַּכָּא). In this case one may hear an echo of {{Genesis 3:19|Gen 3:19}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Study note:* *The divisions of the nighttime*. The ancient Israelites divided the night into distinct periods, or “watches.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you bring them to an end [with] sleep.” The Hebrew verb זָרַם (zaram) has traditionally been taken to mean “flood” or “overwhelm” (note the Polel form of a root זרם in {{Psalm 77:17|Ps 77:17}}, where the verb is used of the clouds pouring down rain). However, the verb form here is Qal, not Polel, and is better understood as a homonym meaning “to make an end [of life].” The term שֵׁנָה (shenah, “sleep”) can be taken as an adverbial accusative; it is a euphemism here for death (see {{Psalm 76:5|Ps 76:5-6}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “flourishes.” The verb is used of a crown shining in {{Psalm 132:18|Ps 132:18}}. Perhaps here in {{Psalm 90:6|Ps 90:6}} it refers to the glistening of the grass in the morning dew.

*Translator's note:* The Polel form of this verb occurs only here. Perhaps the form should be emended to a Qal (which necessitates eliminating the final ל [lamed] as dittographic). See {{Psalm 37:2|Ps 37:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we finish our years like a sigh.” In {{Ezekiel 2:10|Ezek 2:10}} the word הֶגֶה (hegeh) elsewhere refers to a grumbling or moaning sound. Here a brief sigh or moan is probably in view. If so, the simile pictures one’s lifetime as transient. Another option is that the simile alludes to the weakness that characteristically overtakes a person at the end of one’s lifetime. In this case the phrase could be translated, “we end our lives with a painful moan.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the days of our years, in them [are] 70 years.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their pride [is] destruction and wickedness.” The Hebrew noun רֹהַב (rohav) occurs only here. BDB 923 s.v. assigns the meaning “pride,” deriving the noun from the verbal root רָהַב (rahav, “to act stormily [boisterously, arrogantly]”). Here the “pride” of one’s days (see v. {{Psalm 90:9|9}}) probably refers to one’s most productive years in the prime of life. The words translated “destruction and wickedness” are also paired in {{Psalm 10:7|Ps 10:7}}. They also appear in proximity in {{Psalm 7:14|Pss 7:14}} and {{Psalm 55:10|55:10}}. The oppressive and abusive actions of evil men are probably in view (see {{Job 4:8|Job 4:8}}; {{Job 5:6|5:6}}; {{Job 15:35|15:35}}; {{Isaiah 10:1|Isa 10:1}}; {{Isaiah 59:4|59:4}}).

*Study note:* *We fly away*. The psalmist compares life to a bird that quickly flies off (see {{Job 20:8|Job 20:8}}).

*Text-critical note:* *Heb* “and like your fear [is] your raging fury.” Perhaps one should emend וּכְיִרְאָתְךָ (ukheyirʾatekha, “and like your fear”) to יִרְאָתְךְ (yirʾatekha, “your fear”), removing the כ (kaf) as dittography of the kaf ending the previous word. In this case the psalmist asserts “your fear [is] your raging fury,” that is, your raging fury is what causes others to fear you. The suffix on “fear” is understood as objective.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to number our days,” that is, to be aware of how few they really are.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and we will bring a heart of wisdom.” After the imperative of the preceding line, the prefixed verbal form with the conjunction indicates purpose/result. The Hebrew term “heart” here refers to the center of one’s thoughts, volition, and moral character.

*Translator's note:* Elsewhere the Niphal of נָחַם (nakham) + the preposition עַל (ʿal) + a personal object has the nuance “be comforted concerning [the personal object’s death]” (see {{2 Samuel 13:39|2 Sam 13:39}}; Jer 31:15). However, here the context seems to demand “feel sorrow for,” “have pity on.” In {{Deuteronomy 32:36|Deut 32:36}} and {{Psalm 135:14|Ps 135:14}}, where “servants” is also the object of the preposition, this idea is expressed with the Hitpael form of the verb.
